No repositories found. So no execution spec — justified.

Now record the experiment plan. Full fields. Let me craft it carefully.

Title: "Retrieval-time valid-time gating over a clause-level, recency-decoupled amended-regulation benchmark"

research_question: "Does enforcing valid-time (as-of) membership post hoc at retrieval time reduce clause-level point-in-time retrieval failures (returning text not in force at the query date) across sparse, dense and hybrid retrievers, relative to semantic-only retrieval, elapsed-time decay, a hard as-of filter and a retriever adapted to temporal context, and does it improve answer accuracy on queries where version choice changes the answer?"

hypothesis: from D005.

proposed_method: Build the corpus and queries by reconstructing clause version chains with validity intervals; apply a temporal gate post hoc to each base retriever's candidate list; compare signal forms; measure per-cell effects and the interaction; run the answer-differential screen.

baselines: semantic-only per retriever; recency decay; hard as-of filter; published three-signal hybrid (lexical+dense+decay); retriever adapted to temporal context; recency-only ranker; random temporal assignment control.

datasets: (a) primary: a versioned public legal/regulatory corpus with clause-level amendment metadata (e.g., EU consolidated legislation with ELI dates); (b) secondary replication: TempFinRAG-style point-in-time financial QA if obtainable / TemporalESG? Those aren't accessible. Better: propose primary corpus + a secondary domain (e.g., a policy/regulation corpus such as RMA Bhutan circulars used in the regulatory benchmark) to test transfer. Note data availability risk.

workloads: query sets stratified: latest-gold, non-latest-gold (oversampled), answer-differential subset, and a "near-duplicate" subset (high lexical/semantic overlap between versions).

hardware: single machine with one GPU (e.g., 1 × 24GB) for dense encoding/inference; CPU-only feasible for BM25 + small embedding model; reader LLM via API or local 7-8B.

software_environment: Python; rank_bm25/Pyserini for BM25; sentence-transformers with bge-small-en-v1.5 (already used in this line of work); RRF fusion; a fixed reader LLM with a fixed prompt; bootstrap CIs.

metrics: primary — clause-level point-in-time recovery (fraction of queries whose cited passage is in force at target date), version contamination, version confusion; co-primary — answer accuracy on answer-differential subset; diagnostic — nDCG@k, Recall@k, abstention, answer-differential screen pass rate; and the retriever × signal interaction.

ablations: signal form; gate hardness; target-date granularity (day/month/year); validity interval boundary handling (inclusive/exclusive); tie-break; k sweep; chunking.

controls: fixed reader/prompt/k; fixed embedding; fixed query set; random temporal assignment; shuffled validity intervals; recency-only baseline; per-stratum reporting.

confounders_addressed: recency correctness correlation; wording reuse making answers invariant; validity metadata noise; document-granularity vs clause-granularity; retrieval depth k; date granularity; LLM reader variability; corpus snapshot currency.

expected_outcomes: valid-time gating reduces contamination across retrievers with consistent sign; accuracy improves only on answer-differential subset; decay can hurt on long-lived clauses; interaction may show retriever dependence.

failure_conditions: no consistent reduction across retrievers → agnostic claim fails; answer-differential pass rate < ~10% → practical significance limited; semantic-only already near-ceiling on contamination; validity metadata unavailable at clause level (only document-level) → gate degenerates.

reproducibility_notes: pinned corpus snapshot date; document the amendment metadata source; fixed seeds; code+data released; no existing open implementation was found (GitHub searches returned no repositories for point-in-time legal temporal retrieval benchmarks), so the harness must be built; the execution spec is omitted because no repo exists to run.

related_modification_id: M002 (and M005). The field is single: related_modification_id = "M002". related_paper_ids list.

ablations: Temporal signal form: none, recency decay, hard as-of gate, gate plus graded tie-break, published three-signal hybrid
Gate hardness: hard exclusion vs graded penalty for near-valid versions
Validity-interval boundary handling: inclusive vs half-open intervals and same-day amendment/applicability dates
Retrieval depth k and chunk granularity (whole clause vs sub-clause fragments)
Near-duplicate stratum only (versions with high lexical and embedding overlap) to test the intended regime
baselines: Semantic-only retrieval per base retriever (BM25, dense, hybrid RRF) with no temporal term
Recency/elapsed-time decay re-ranking with tuned decay rate
Published fixed three-signal hybrid (lexical + dense + decay)
Retriever adapted to temporal context (date-conditioned or fine-tuned dense retriever)
Recency-only ranker (always prefer the latest version), reported per stratum
Random temporal assignment control (random validity intervals)
confounders_addressed: Recency is confounded with correctness on most naturally occurring queries - addressed by the oversampled non-latest-gold stratum and a recency-only ranker
Wording reuse can make answers identical across versions so accuracy is blind to version confusion - addressed by the answer-differential screen and version-identity labels
Document-granularity validity metadata would make the gate a coarse filter - addressed by requiring clause-level intervals and reporting the fraction resolvable at clause vs document level
Retrieval depth k can mask re-ranking effects - k held fixed across arms with a small sweep reported
Reader variability could drive answer differences - same reader, prompt, temperature and decoding for every arm
Corpus snapshot currency can make not-yet-in-force text look like gold - snapshot pinned and documented
controls: Same query set, target-date annotations, corpus snapshot and preprocessing in every arm
Same embedding model, chunking, k and reader LLM with a fixed prompt template
Paired comparisons over identical queries with bootstrap confidence intervals
Per-stratum reporting (latest-gold, non-latest-gold, answer-differential, near-duplicate) rather than pooled averages
Pre-registered consistency criterion for the retrieval-agnostic claim (same sign and non-trivial effect in every retriever cell)
Baselines and method evaluated on the same machine and environment
datasets: Primary: a public versioned legal/regulatory corpus with clause-level amendment metadata and machine-readable validity dates (e.g. consolidated EU legislation with European Legislation Identifier entry-into-force and applicability dates), snapshotted on a fixed date
Primary query set: time-stamped questions constructed from clause version chains, with an oversampled non-latest-gold stratum and an answer-differential subset
Replication (if obtainable): a second domain corpus of amended regulatory/policy text to test transfer, e.g. central-bank circulars of the kind used in regulatory retrieval benchmarking
Not used: TemporalESG and the trilingual ESG benchmark (accessibility and domain mismatch), SituatedQA/TimeQA (web QA, not clause-versioned)
input.expected_outcomes: Valid-time gating reduces clause-level contamination and point-in-time failures relative to semantic-only retrieval and relative to elapsed-time decay in most or all retriever cells, with the largest gains on the non-latest-gold and near-duplicate strata; elapsed-time decay is expected to underperform and can actively harm long-lived in-force clauses; answer accuracy improves only on the answer-differential subset and remains flat elsewhere; the recency-only ranker matches the temporal layer on the latest-gold stratum, which is reported as an expected boundary condition rather than a failure.
failure_conditions: No consistent reduction in contamination across the three retriever families (sign or significance varies by retriever) - the retrieval-agnostic claim is not supported
Semantic-only retrieval already achieves near-ceiling point-in-time recovery on the non-latest stratum - the problem is not real in this corpus
Answer-differential screen pass rate is very low (order of a few percent), so contamination reductions cannot be shown to change user-visible answers - practical significance not supported
Clause-level validity intervals cannot be recovered and only document-level dates exist, so the gate cannot address version ambiguity within a document
The retriever adapted to temporal context dominates the post-hoc gate on every stratum - the training-free plug-in framing is not competitive
input.hardware: Single workstation with one 24 GB GPU for dense encoding and any local reader model; BM25 and hybrid arms are CPU-feasible. If a hosted reader LLM is used, a fixed API budget with cached responses. No cluster or distributed training required for the training-free arms; the retriever-adapted arm needs one GPU for fine-tuning.
input.hypothesis: Applying a valid-time (as-of) gate post hoc reduces clause-level point-in-time retrieval failures across sparse, dense and hybrid base retrievers, with the same sign and a non-trivial effect size in each retriever family, and comparably to or better than a retriever adapted to temporal context; the reduction in contamination translates into improved answer accuracy specifically on queries where retrieving a non-gold version would change the reference answer, and not on queries whose versions are answer-equivalent.
metrics: Primary: clause-level point-in-time recovery - fraction of queries whose top-ranked or cited passage was in force at the target date
Primary: version contamination - fraction of retrieved passages not in force at the target date (superseded or not-yet-in-force)
Primary: version confusion - fraction of queries whose selected version differs from the gold version
Co-primary: answer accuracy (EM/F1 or judged equivalence) on the answer-differential subset only
Diagnostic: nDCG@k and Recall@k against version-identity gold labels
Diagnostic: abstention rate when no version is in force at the target date
Interaction: retriever x temporal-signal effect estimate with paired bootstrap confidence intervals
input.proposed_method: Reconstruct clause version chains from amendment metadata and derive validity intervals; construct time-stamped queries from those chains with gold labelled by version identity, deliberately oversampling queries whose in-force version is not the latest. Screen queries for answer-differential sensitivity by obtaining a reference answer under each candidate version with the fixed reader, and report the pass rate. For each base retriever (BM25, dense, hybrid RRF) obtain a candidate list at fixed depth, then apply the temporal layer post hoc in four signal forms (none, recency decay, hard valid-time gate, gate plus graded tie-break) so the base retriever is untouched. Compare cells with paired bootstrap confidence intervals over queries, report the retriever x signal interaction and per-stratum results, and include a retriever adapted to temporal context as a representation-level comparator.
input.reproducibility_notes: No open implementation was found to build on: GitHub searches for a point-in-time legal temporal retrieval benchmark and for a SituatedQA-style time-sensitive retrieval benchmark returned no repositories, so the benchmark and harness must be built and released. Therefore no execution spec is attached - there is no repository to clone and no existing artifact whose commands could write metrics.json. Reproducibility measures for when it is built: pin and document the corpus snapshot date and amendment metadata source, publish version chains and validity intervals, fix all seeds, hold the reader/prompt/decoding fixed, publish the answer-differential screening procedure and the exact query-stratum assignments, release per-query predictions so any metric can be recomputed, and report paired bootstrap confidence intervals for every comparison.
input.research_question: Does enforcing valid-time (as-of) membership post hoc at retrieval time reduce clause-level point-in-time retrieval failures (returning text not in force at the query date) across sparse, dense and hybrid retrievers - relative to semantic-only retrieval, elapsed-time decay, a hard as-of filter, and a retriever adapted to temporal context - and does it improve answer accuracy on the subset of queries where retrieving a non-gold version would change the answer?
input.title: Retrieval-time valid-time gating over a clause-level, recency-decoupled amended-regulation benchmark
workloads: Time-stamped queries over clause version chains, stratified into latest-gold and non-latest-gold (oversampled) strata
Answer-differential subset: queries where at least one non-gold version yields a different reference answer
Near-duplicate subset: queries whose competing versions share high lexical overlap and embedding similarity
No-version-in-force queries where the correct behaviour is to abstain or state absence
Retrieval depth k in the small-to-moderate range typical of RAG pipelines, with k held fixed across arms

input.confidence_basis: No retrieved work quantifies answer sensitivity to clause version, and the quantity is a property of the corpus, so it cannot be settled by further reading of the existing set; the experimental design now measures it directly as the screen pass rate.
input.resolution: Partially resolved by design: the literature cannot answer this, so the experiment plan makes the answer-differential screen pass rate a reported primary quantity, computed by obtaining a reference answer under each candidate version with a fixed reader and marking a query answer-differential when the gold version's answer differs from at least one competing version's answer. The plan also makes the consequence explicit in its failure conditions: if the pass rate is only a few percent, contamination reductions cannot be shown to change user-visible answers and the practical-significance claim fails. The value remains unknown until the screen is run.
